deliverables.text: A Human-Poll Standings Table -- AP Top 25 rank, record, AP voting points, and percent of maximum possible AP voting points per team, plus one original visual of the top ten teams' percent-of-maximum.
A Computer Power-Rating Table -- conference, record, SRS, and percent of the season's single highest SRS per team, plus one original visual ranking teams by SRS.
A Composite Selection Score Table -- for the two contested teams plus 3+ comparison teams, the mean of each team's Human% and Machine% scores, arithmetic shown.
A Supporting-Evidence Brief -- 5+ additional data points beyond D1-D3's percentages, at least one itself a calculated mean.

appendices.title: How the Selection Committee Has Actually Voted

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA4 (Appendix F) already states in prose that the 50/50 weighting between the Human and Machine scores is 'the single most load-bearing assumption in the case... a materially different weighting... changes which option the composite favors' and is 'flagged for the +/-50% sensitivity flex.' A +50% flex (human_weight -> 0.75) does flip the winner to Oklahoma, and a -50% flex (-> 0.25) widens Michigan's margin past the 20% cap -- exactly the disclosed, expected behavior, not an undiscovered defect. The CFP committee itself uses no fixed-weight formula (Appendix D), so no single weighting is more 'correct' than another; that irreducible, disclosed subjectivity is the case's real teaching point, not something a different constant would fix.

MA2 (Appendix F) states the Human% denominator is the maximum possible AP poll score (63 voters x 25 points = 1,575), confirmed directly from Georgia's own perfect first-place total in the source data. Flexing this +-50% is a scenario/what-if stress test of 'what if the poll had a different voter count or scale,' not a real ambiguity in this season's actual, sourced poll structure -- the real AP poll's voter count is fixed and known, this dial only exists to satisfy SPEC's uniform +-50%-flex-every-stated-assumption requirement, not because the true value is in doubt.

MA3 (Appendix F) states the Machine% denominator is the highest SRS in the full ~130-team dataset (Georgia, 25.94), confirmed by direct computation, and is flagged in Appendix F itself as 'one of the two most load-bearing assumptions' because the ceiling team (Georgia) is not one of the two contested options, so its exact rating affects Oklahoma and Michigan asymmetrically. A -50% flex breaks the 20% cap by construction (halving the ceiling roughly doubles every team's Machine%, and Michigan's real SRS is proportionally much closer to that ceiling than Oklahoma's is) -- this is the expected, already-named behavior of a disclosed asymmetric-denominator choice, not new instability.

balance.argument_a: Oklahoma is undefeated (9-0), the only team ranked AP #4 or better with a zero in the loss column, and sits at roughly 87.7% of the maximum possible AP voting points -- near-unanimous human consensus. The committee's own real 2014-2023 track record backs this instinct: 32 of the 40 selected teams in the four-team era were power-conference champions, and no team with two or more losses was ever selected (Appendix D). Trusting the accumulated human judgment behind that pattern over a single formula's opinion is a defensible, evidence-backed stance.
balance.argument_b: Michigan's SRS (21.02) is the second-highest of the ~130-team full dataset -- only Georgia's is higher -- reflecting dominant point differentials against a real schedule that the human poll (AP #9, only 66.5% of maximum voting points) has been slow to recognize. This is precisely the historical complaint (poll voters anchored on preseason reputation and name-brand recognition) that produced the BCS and then the CFP committee system in the first place. Under this case's own neutral, equally-weighted Composite Selection Score, Michigan leads Oklahoma by about 11.7%, because Michigan's human-poll deficit is proportionally smaller than Oklahoma's SRS deficit.
balance.margin_basis: Computed as 100*|A-B|/min(A,B) on each team's Composite Selection Score (mean of Human% of max AP points and Machine% of the dataset's highest SRS). Oklahoma composite ~66.08 (Human 87.75%, Machine 44.41%); Michigan composite ~73.79 (Human 66.54%, Machine 81.03%).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The committee's eleven already-decided spots are fixed; only the twelfth, contested spot is modeled.
modeling_assumptions.basis: Narrows the real, many-candidate 12-team selection process down to the two-team decision named in the human-approved locked dilemma (Oklahoma vs. Michigan).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Not numerically load-bearing; a scoping choice, not a modeled quantity.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: A team's Human score is AP voting points as a percent of the maximum possible (63 first-place voters x 25 points).
modeling_assumptions.basis: The 63-voter count is confirmed directly within the source data itself: Georgia's 1,575-point total equals exactly 63 x 25, and the workbook labels Georgia '(63)' for first-place votes.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Directly sets every team's Human% in Appendix B and every downstream composite score.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: A team's Machine score is SRS as a percent of the single highest SRS rating in the full national dataset.
modeling_assumptions.basis: Georgia's SRS is the highest of all ~130 FBS teams in the bundled workbook, confirmed by direct computation over the full dataset.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: One of the two most load-bearing assumptions -- the ceiling team (Georgia) is not itself one of the two contested options, so using it as the denominator affects Oklahoma and Michigan differently since their SRS gaps to Georgia differ in absolute terms.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The Composite Selection Score is the unweighted (50/50) mean of the Human score and the Machine score.
modeling_assumptions.basis: A modeling choice made for this exercise to give students a single comparable number; not an official CFP formula (the CFP committee itself uses no fixed-weight formula at all, per Appendix D).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The single most load-bearing assumption in the case -- flagged for the +/-50% sensitivity flex (Tier 2 probe 3). A materially different weighting (e.g., weighting the human score more heavily, matching the committee's own real historical bias toward clean records) changes which option the composite favors.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The case is set in a fictional near-future December Selection Sunday; the underlying poll and power-rating figures are drawn from a real, historical FBS season's dataset, reused here for real, internally consistent numbers.
modeling_assumptions.basis: The original source docx's own narrative was written generically (no real season pinned down); this conversion follows the locked-dilemma file's guidance to substitute the real, bundled 2021 dataset directly rather than inventing fictional numbers of the same shape.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Not numerically load-bearing; a narrative-framing choice, consistent with the precedent set by cases/electoral-college (real EV apportionment reused in a fictional 2044 election).

twist_recompute_alabama_ceiling.note: Twist reframes the SRS ceiling from Georgia (25.94, the presumptive #1 overall seed and not itself a competitor for this spot) to Alabama (20.95, the highest SRS among teams genuinely in the at-large conversation).

sensitivity_note: The Composite Selection Score's 50/50 weighting (MA4) and the choice of SRS ceiling (MA3, Georgia -- a team not itself one of the two contested options) are this case's most load-bearing assumptions; both are flagged for the +/-50% sensitivity flex (Tier 2 probe 3). SPEC section 6 does not otherwise apply -- the case's stakes are athletic postseason selection, not death/illness/financial hardship.
legacy_conversion_note: Original sources: source/Y2/Session 4/College Football Playoff Committee/Case Study_ College Football Playoff Committee.docx and Guides Notes.docx (both read in full via python-docx), plus the bundled 2021 College Football Statistics.xlsx Appendix B workbook (read directly via openpyxl, both sheets). The Case Study docx's own narrative was written generically (a dominant SEC champion, an undefeated Big Ten team, etc., never named) and centered on a 12-team, many-candidate selection ('which 12 teams do you invite'); the Guide Notes docx (an earlier, 4-team-era version of the same case, different protagonist Paola Boivin) is the one that explicitly poses the framing question this case is built around: 'do you believe that machines or humans would be better at determining the best teams in college football.' Per the human-approved lock in cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md's college-football-playoff-committee entry, the case is narrowed from the open 12-team selection down to a single, concrete binary over the committee's one contested final spot: Oklahoma (trust the human AP poll) vs. Michigan (trust the computer SRS rating), with the protagonist originally taken from the Case Study docx's own named real committee member; per the same personality-rights concern already applied to cases/movie-producer's conversion (attaching an invented, dramatized internal deliberation and fabricated career biography to a real, still-serving committee member's name serves no mathematical purpose and is an unnecessary risk), this conversion instead uses a fictional protagonist, Derek Talcott, with a fictional (non-matching) career biography. One factual correction against the lock file's own draft description: the lock's prose describes Michigan's SRS as 'the third-highest computer rating in the entire dataset'; direct computation over the full ~130-team 2021 Team Stats sheet shows Michigan's SRS (21.02) is actually the second-highest (Georgia 25.94, Michigan 21.02, Alabama 20.95) -- the binary options (A: Oklahoma, B: Michigan) and their cited stats are unchanged from the lock, only the ordinal descriptor 'third-highest' was corrected to the verified 'second-highest' in this case's own Background/case.json text. The Human/Machine percent-of-maximum comparison, the resulting Composite Selection Score, and its 11.67% margin favoring Michigan are new, added to force real percent and mean skills the source's own open-ended 'which 12 teams' prompt did not itself require -- new_coverage[] is legitimately empty because every skill these real deliverables force (percent, convert-numbers-to-percents, mean, find-the-mean-of-a-set-of-data) already has coverage elsewhere in the spine; no zero-n skill in the spine (geometry volumes, calculus derivatives, discrete-math set theory/logic) has an honest connection to a poll-vs-power-rating comparison built entirely from real win-loss/point-differential data. The original source's own '$488 million' CFP payout figure (Guide Notes docx) was not independently verifiable and is not reused; a real, sourced $1.3 billion 2026 media-rights figure (CBS Sports, source S6) is cited instead where playoff financial stakes are mentioned, and it is not load-bearing to any calculation. The original source's '38 of 40' four-team-era selection statistic could not be independently verified in this research pass and is NOT reused (an initial attempt to substitute a '32 of 40' Wikipedia-attributed figure was itself found unverifiable and factually doubtful during a second-pass check -- Alabama's 2017 at-large selection over Big Ten champion Ohio State, without having won its own conference that year, is a well-documented counterexample to any claim that every non-exception CFP spot in the four-team era went to a conference champion -- so that specific statistic was dropped from Appendix D/source S3 entirely rather than repeating an unverified number, per SPEC section 5).
